claim as made in prose: Strava's updated Global Heatmap visualized two years of trailing exercise data from athletes worldwide
source: Robb, "Building the Global Heatmap", Strava Engineering, 2017-11-01 (strava-building-heatmap.txt)

claim as made in prose: The dataset comprised 700 million activities, 1.4 trillion lat/long points, 7.7 trillion rasterized pixels, 5 terabytes of raw data, 16 billion kilometers, and 100,000 years of activity
source: Robb, "Building the Global Heatmap", Strava Engineering, 2017-11-01 (strava-building-heatmap.txt)

claim as made in prose: Strava presented the Global Heatmap as a resource for athletes to discover places to exercise
source: Hassan et al., USENIX Security 2018, §7.1 (hassan-fitness-trackers.txt); Strava, "Heatmap Updates" (strava-heatmap-updates.txt)

claim as made in prose: The heatmap only contained public activities and respected all user privacy settings
source: Robb, "Building the Global Heatmap", Strava Engineering, 2017-11-01 (strava-building-heatmap.txt)

claim as made in prose: Cleanup filters removed unreasonable running speeds and used a higher cycling ceiling to exclude cars and planes
source: Robb, "Building the Global Heatmap", Strava Engineering, 2017-11-01 (strava-building-heatmap.txt)

claim as made in prose: The Guardian published a headline claiming Strava gave away the location of secret US army bases
source: The Guardian, 2018-01-28 (guardian-folk.txt)

claim as made in prose: Wikipedia recorded that in January 2018 an Australian student discovered the map had mapped military bases in Syria, Afghanistan, and HMNB Clyde
source: Wikipedia, "Strava", §Military breaches (wikipedia-folk.txt)

claim as made in prose: Data Science in Context (Spector, Norvig, Wiggins, Wing, 2022 draft): Strava did nothing wrong, anonymized tracks for opted-in users
source: data-science-context-folk.txt; title page of the PDF read 2026-09-03 for the authors

claim as made in prose: Quarles emphasized that Strava respected privacy selections, including an existing ability to opt out of heatmaps altogether
source: Quarles, "A Letter to the Strava Community", 2018-01-29 (strava-letter.txt)

claim as made in prose: Quarles said military members and humanitarian workers may have shared sparse-area locations and inadvertently increased awareness of sensitive locations
source: Quarles, "A Letter to the Strava Community", 2018-01-29 (strava-letter.txt)

claim as made in prose: Quarles wrote that Strava understood its responsibility for shared data and would review motivational features against abuse by people with bad intent
source: Quarles, "A Letter to the Strava Community", 2018-01-29 (strava-letter.txt)

claim as made in prose: Senators Coons and Flake pressed Strava, stating consumers were confused by opt-outs and data could be cross-referenced
source: Coons and Flake letter to Strava CEO, 2018-02-14 (coons-flake-letter.txt)

claim as made in prose: Strava shifted the heatmap to a monthly refresh schedule to remove opted-out contributions at the next update
source: Strava, "Heatmap Updates", archived 2018-07-19 (strava-heatmap-updates.txt; the excerpt carries no post date)

claim as made in prose: Strava required several different athletes before showing heat on low-activity roads and trails
source: Strava, "Heatmap Updates", archived 2018-07-19 (strava-heatmap-updates.txt; the excerpt carries no post date)

claim as made in prose: Strava restricted street-level zoom details on the public heatmap to registered Strava athletes
source: Strava, "Heatmap Updates", archived 2018-07-19 (strava-heatmap-updates.txt; the excerpt carries no post date)

claim as made in prose: Strava replaced one-pixel GPS points with paths connecting successive points and raised the highest resolution from 4 meters to 2 meters
source: Robb, "Building the Global Heatmap", Strava Engineering, 2017-11-01 (strava-building-heatmap.txt)

claim as made in prose: Strava used the cumulative distribution function so a pixel represented the percentage of pixels with lower heat, producing a uniform colormap distribution
source: Robb, "Building the Global Heatmap", Strava Engineering, 2017-11-01 (strava-building-heatmap.txt)

claim as made in prose: Strava noted CDF normalization maximized relative contrast locally, so identical colors did not represent identical activity counts globally
source: Robb, "Building the Global Heatmap", Strava Engineering, 2017-11-01 (strava-building-heatmap.txt)

claim as made in prose: Hassan et al. established that background noise sparsity in remote regions caused the heatmap to leak sensitive sites and patrol routes
source: Hassan et al., USENIX Security 2018, §7.1 (hassan-fitness-trackers.txt)

claim as made in prose: Hassan et al. documented that the identities of specific athletes were not directly leaked within the heatmap itself
source: Hassan et al., USENIX Security 2018, §7.1 (hassan-fitness-trackers.txt)

claim as made in prose: Hassan et al. demonstrated an adjacent method using spoofed GPS data to discover athlete IDs in a given area
source: Hassan et al., USENIX Security 2018, §7.1 (hassan-fitness-trackers.txt)

claim as made in prose: Ars Technica published a headline reporting the Pentagon told troops to turn off fitness tracker GPS in warzones
source: Ars Technica, August 2018 (ars-folk.txt; month from the URL, no date line in the excerpt)

claim as made in prose: Deputy Secretary Shanahan's memorandum prohibited personnel from using geolocation features and functionality in operational areas
source: DoD Memorandum, 2018-08-03, p. 1 (dod-geolocation-memo.txt)

claim as made in prose: Combatant Commanders could authorize geolocation on non-government devices in operational areas after an OPSEC survey under Directive 5205.02E
source: DoD Memorandum, 2018-08-03, p. 1 (dod-geolocation-memo.txt)

claim as made in prose: Commanders could authorize geolocation on government-issued devices in operational areas based on mission necessity considering OPSEC risks
source: DoD Memorandum, 2018-08-03, p. 1 (dod-geolocation-memo.txt)

claim as made in prose: Outside operational areas, DoD component heads were instructed to consider risks and apply a tiered location sensitivity framework
source: DoD Memorandum, 2018-08-03, pp. 1–2 (dod-geolocation-memo.txt)

claim as made in prose: GAO reported DoD's 2016 policy warned that aggregated IoT data could inform adversaries about unit capabilities, deployments, or overtime
GAO found that comprehensive threat-based OPSEC surveys examining IoT risks were not being conducted despite Directive 5205.02E
DoD concurred with GAO's recommendation to conduct OPSEC surveys addressing IoT risks under existing policies
Strava adopted randomized spatial cloaking for user-specified Privacy Zones; the paper says it significantly increases the complexity of endpoint inference and may dissuade attackers
source: Hassan et al., USENIX Security 2018, §§7.1, 9 (hassan-fitness-trackers.txt)

claim as made in prose: The sources collected for this chapter contain no follow-up measurement of sensitive-site visibility or compliance with the DoD directive as of 2026-09-03
source: Chapter source inventory and the documents listed in resources/sources/06/SOURCES.md, read 2026-09-03

claim as made in prose: The two-page memorandum was issued on 3 August 2018 from the Office of the Deputy Secretary of Defense
source: DoD Memorandum, header and pp. 1–2 (dod-geolocation-memo.txt)

claim as made in prose: Robb's saved account discusses filters and visual quality, including that CDF normalization "looks really nice," but does not describe a threat model for readers examining sparse traces
source: Robb, "Building the Global Heatmap" (strava-building-heatmap.txt), Input Data and Filtering and Heat Normalization

claim as made in prose: Other athletes recording within an athlete's Privacy Zone may create heat on the map through that zone
source: Strava, "Heatmap Updates" (strava-heatmap-updates.txt), privacy controls list
